lanes.title: EEOC federal-sector EEO process rule
lanes.latest: Proposed rule published Aug. 28, 2026 after a 2–1 Commission vote on Aug. 26. It would end mandatory pre-complaint counseling, make administrative judge hearings discretionary, and bar administrative class complaints. Comments close Sept. 28.

timeline.text: EEOC votes to rescind 2024 harassment enforcement guidance.
EEOC overturns Lusardi v. McHugh restroom-access precedent for federal employees.
AFGE and two federal employees sue EEOC over an internal freeze on processing federal-sector class complaints.
Commission votes 2–1 to advance the proposed rule.
Proposed rule published in the Federal Register; 30-day comment period.

next: AFGE / WFP comment filed by Sept. 28
Comment volume and allied filings on the docket
Ruling in AFGE's class-complaint freeze suit
lanes.relevance: This rule sets the process a federal employee uses to file a discrimination complaint against their agency, including a complaint about a job decision made under H.R. 10319 if it became law. The proposal would end administrative class complaints.

lanes.title: Military gender-dysphoria service ban litigation
lanes.ids: EO 14183 (Jan. 27, 2025) · Talbott v. United States · Shilling v. United States
lanes.latest: DOJ petitioned the Supreme Court on Aug. 28, 2026 to review Talbott before trial, after a divided D.C. Circuit panel in June kept currently serving transgender troops protected from discharge. The ban on new accessions remains in effect.

timeline.text: Talbott: Judge Ana Reyes (D.D.C.) issues nationwide preliminary injunction.
Shilling: Supreme Court stays that injunction, allowing the ban to take effect while litigation continues.
Shilling: Ninth Circuit hears oral argument; decision pending.
Talbott: divided D.C. Circuit panel blocks discharge of currently serving plaintiffs; allows restrictions on new recruits.
Talbott: district court certifies a class of transgender service members (reported July 2).
Talbott: DOJ files Supreme Court petition seeking review before trial.

next: Supreme Court action on the Talbott petition
lanes.relevance: The military policy uses the same approach as H.R. 10319: a gender dysphoria diagnosis as the basis for disqualification. These cases are testing whether that approach is lawful.

lanes.title: Schedule Policy/Career (formerly Schedule F)
lanes.ids: OPM final rule (Feb. 6, 2026) · EO of June 3, 2026
lanes.latest: OPM finalized the rule Feb. 6, 2026, and a June 3 executive order moved positions into the new schedule. AFGE is a plaintiff in challenges; district-court injunctions have been stayed on appeal, so the policy remains in effect.

timeline.text: Schedule F revived by executive order; AFGE/AFSCME and NTEU file suits.
OPM publishes Schedule Policy/Career final rule.
Coalition suit (PEER, AFGE, AFSCME, AFL-CIO; Democracy Forward) challenges the order and final rule.
EO “Implementing Schedule Policy/Career in the Excepted Service” moves positions into the schedule.

next: Appellate merits ruling in any challenge
Whether covered safety/security positions are reclassified
lanes.relevance: Employees moved into Schedule Policy/Career lose the adverse-action appeal rights that normally apply when an agency removes a career employee. Estimates of positions affected vary by source (about 8,000 under the June order; up to 50,000 overall).

openQuestions: What triggers agency knowledge of a diagnosis, and does that inquiry comply with Rehabilitation Act limits?
For a current employee: removal, reassignment, or something else — and what appeal rights apply?
Is there any path to show the diagnosis doesn't affect job performance, or is it a strict bar?
Which positions and certifications government-wide already carry a mental-health standard, and at how many agencies?
Would AFGE have a formal consultation role in the 180-day agency rulemaking?

changeLog.text: Tracker created. Baseline verified against Congress.gov (data updated Sept. 14), Federal Register, and case counsel pages. No bill movement since referral.
Site reorganized into five pages with a plain-language overview; “Why it matters” notes rewritten as factual “How it connects” notes.

plain.label: What it does
plain.text: If a federal job or license already requires passing a mental-health fitness standard, a gender dysphoria diagnosis would automatically disqualify the person — no matter how well they do the job.

plain.label: Who it reaches
plain.text: People diagnosed with gender dysphoria who hold or want those jobs or licenses. The wording could reach current employees, not just applicants. It is not a rule for every federal worker.

plain.label: Where it stands
plain.text: Introduced Sept. 8, 2026 and sent to the House Oversight Committee. No cosponsors and no hearing. It is not law.

plain.label: If it passed
plain.text: Each agency would have 180 days to write the rules for how it works. The bill doesn't say how agencies would learn of a diagnosis or what happens to current employees.
